title: Edge Walker
context: Grade 5, the recap and the pages on the perimeter of a rectangle. An adult sees a formula. What the pages are doing is measuring a boundary: the perimeter is the length of the boundary, every side is added once and in one unit, and a rectangle's two equal pairs of sides let the sum be written as two lots of one length and one breadth.

writeup.why: Find a perimeter as the length of a boundary by adding every side once, in one unit, name the longer side of a rectangle its length, and fold its four sides into 2 x (length + breadth).
writeup.look: A figure on squared paper with its sides labelled, an ant at one corner, a Sum strip along the foot of the working area, and on the later phases the Length and Breadth tags and the Two lots button.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Edge Walker' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of sides walked out of the number the figure has. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The figure lies on squared paper at x 120, y 230, inside a box 620 by 380, drawn to one scale, each side labelled deep blue with its length and unit. The ant is a small drawn figure 40 across that the child drags along the boundary; each side it walks lights vermilion, labelled Boundary. The Sum strip runs along y 650 from x 120, 900 long, and takes each side's length as a tile in the order walked. The Write in cm tile waits at x 800, y 250, and the unit fact it writes appears in ink beside the side it lands on. The Length and Breadth tags wait at x 800, y 340, each a rounded label. The Two lots button stands at x 800, y 430, and the line it writes, 2 x (length + breadth), sits above the Sum strip at y 600. The perimeter reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a cm key and an m key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last figure stays drawn with its boundary vermilion, the Sum strip under it and the perimeter in green with its unit.

writeup.delight: When the ant closes the boundary on the first phase, it gives a small hop at the corner where it started, and the whole vermilion path glows once before the sum lands.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet walked. On the first phase the five-sided bed lies on the squared paper with the ant at one corner and the Sum strip empty. source_tool.description: A figure is drawn on squared paper, every side to one scale and labelled deep blue with its length and unit. A small ant sits at one corner. The child drags the ant along the boundary: each side it walks lights vermilion, labelled Boundary, and that side's length drops into a Sum strip along the foot of the working area, in the order walked. A side walked a second time drops in a second time, and a side skipped leaves a gap in the vermilion path. A Write in cm tile, dragged onto a side given in metres, rewrites it in centimetres and writes the unit fact 1 m = 100 cm beside it in ink. Length and Breadth tags can be dragged onto the sides of a rectangle. A Two lots button slides one length and one breadth together, writes 2 x (length + breadth) above the strip, and doubles the pair. A number pad types a length with a cm or m key. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of sides walked out of the number the figure has.
source_tool.art_direction: An ant walking a garden bed / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it

zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Draw a shape and walk the ant round it.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: Two lots of length and breadth

placement.where: After the class has run a finger and then a string once round a book, a slate and a lid, and laid the string along a metre scale. The tool is what drops each side's length into a sum as it is walked, which a finished drawing cannot do.

answer_key.rule: The perimeter of a figure is the length of its boundary: add every side once, in one unit. Sides in two units are written in one unit first, and 1 m = 100 cm. The longer side of a rectangle is its length and the shorter side is its breadth, and opposite sides are equal. So the perimeter of a rectangle is length + breadth + length + breadth, which is 2 x (length + breadth). A perimeter is a length, in cm or m.
answer_key.wrong: The ant walks the boundary again, slowly, beside the child's sum, and each side lights vermilion as its length is added; the side the child missed, doubled or left in another unit is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Walk the boundary once, side by side: 14 m, 9 m, 11 m, 7 m and 10 m.
The perimeter is the length of the boundary, so it is 51 m.
items.question: A five-sided flower bed has sides of 14 m, 9 m, 11 m, 7 m and 10 m. What is its perimeter?
items.checkpoint: A perimeter is a length, so its unit is m or cm.
items.misconception: Counting the sides instead of adding their lengths, and giving the number of sides as the answer.

steps: The sides are in two units, so write every side in cm first.
1 m = 100 cm, so the first side is 100 cm.
items.question: A mat has sides of 1 m, 85 cm, 90 cm and 75 cm. What is its perimeter in cm?
items.checkpoint: Put every side in one unit before adding.
items.misconception: Adding the four numbers as they stand, which treats the metre as one centimetre and gives a perimeter far too short.

steps: The longer side of a rectangle is its length, so the length is 11 cm.
The shorter side is the breadth, so the breadth is 6 cm.
Opposite sides are equal, so walk 11 cm, 6 cm, 11 cm and 6 cm.
So the perimeter of a rectangle 11 cm long and 6 cm wide is 11 + 6 + 11 + 6 = 34 cm.
items.answer: The length is 11 cm, and the perimeter is 34 cm
items.question: A rectangle has sides of 11 cm and 6 cm. Which side is its length, and what is its perimeter?
items.checkpoint: Name the longer side the length before adding.
items.misconception: Adding only the two sides that are labelled, which walks only half of the boundary.

steps: Add one length and one breadth: 15 + 8 = 23.
Take two lots of it: 2 x 23 = 46.
So the perimeter of a rectangle 15 m long and 8 m wide is 2 x (15 + 8) = 46 m.
Check it by walking all four sides: 15 + 8 + 15 + 8 = 46.
items.question: A rectangle is 15 m long and 8 m wide. Find its perimeter by the formula.
items.checkpoint: The brackets say add first, then double.
items.misconception: Doubling only the length and then adding one breadth, which leaves one breadth out of the walk.

A rectangle has sides of 12 cm and 5 cm. Which side is its length?
items.final_answer: The 12 cm side, because the longer side is the length

items.question: A three-sided garden bed has sides of 2 m, 150 cm and 180 cm. What is its perimeter in cm?

items.final_answer: The perimeter of a rectangle 17 cm long and 7 cm wide is 17 + 7 + 17 + 7 = 48 cm

items.question: Use the formula to find the perimeter of a rectangle 21 m long and 14 m wide.
items.final_answer: The perimeter of a rectangle 21 m long and 14 m wide is 2 x (21 + 14) = 70 m

teaching_notes: Run a finger, then a string, once round a real edge before the tool opens. Say that the perimeter is the length of the boundary every time, so it is never taken for the edge itself. Put every side in one unit first and say the unit fact aloud. Name the longer side of a rectangle its length before any formula, and check the formula against all four sides added. Use beds, cards, frames and gardens for the figures; the printed exercises' own lengths are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build an edge walker tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A figure is drawn to one scale on squared paper, each side labelled deep blue with its length and unit. The child drags a small ant along the boundary; each side it walks lights vermilion, labelled Boundary, and drops its length into a Sum strip in the order walked, so a side walked twice appears twice and a side skipped leaves a gap. A Write in cm tile rewrites a side in metres as centimetres and writes the unit fact 1 m = 100 cm in ink. Length and Breadth tags are dragged onto a rectangle's sides. A Two lots button slides one length and one breadth together and writes 2 x (length + breadth). A number pad types a length with cm and m keys. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the sides walked. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Walk the ant once round the edge. Every side goes into the sum. Put every side in one unit first.
